gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 16-inch MacBook Pro (M5 Pro / M5 Max) drives a 2560x1600 120 Hz portable screen natively from any of its three Thunderbolt 5 ports with its separate MagSafe 3 port left free for the 140 W charger, or that Apple supports variable refresh on such a screen only over USB-C/Thunderbolt and says not to use HDMI.
standout_why: Compared against four pages opened 2026-11-26. Macworld's best-portable-monitors-for-Mac roundup gives the Duex Float 2 Pro's 65 W pass-through and the single-display limit of non-Pro M1/M2 Macs, but nothing on what the 16-inch Pro's ports drive, MagSafe, or HDMI versus USB-C. Macworld's espresso Pro review gives a 13 W draw and 100 W pass-through but no Mac-side limits. PCWorld only recommends 'a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alternate Mode and USB Power Delivery'. Three cited pages could not be compared: the RTINGS and TechRadar fetches returned only navigation or one truncated pick, and seattlepi.com refused the fetch. ChatGPT's own answer warns that pass-through may not fully power a 16-inch Pro but never says the charger can go into MagSafe instead.
decides: It confirms the plan works without a driver: Apple lists DisplayPort on all three Thunderbolt 5 ports and up to three external displays at 4K 144 Hz on the M5 Pro, so a 2560x1600 120 Hz or 144 Hz panel sits inside the Mac's limits. It removes pass-through wattage as a ranking factor for this laptop, because the 140 W charger has its own MagSafe 3 port; the Float 2 Pro's 65 W pass-through is neither a plus nor a limit here. It makes the USB-C cable the one to use for 120 Hz with Adaptive Sync, so a FreeSync panel (the UPERFECT GR16EQ lead) gets variable refresh on the Mac only over USB-C, not mini HDMI. The pick order still rests on refresh, brightness and weight; I could not re-read those store pages today (HTTP 429), so this angle does not confirm them.

findings.label: Current 16-inch MacBook Pro chips and video path on its USB-C ports
findings.value: M5 Pro or M5 Max; 'Three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports with support for: Charging, DisplayPort, Thunderbolt 5 (up to 120Gb/s), USB 4'; 'Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports support native DisplayPort 2.1 speeds'
findings.note: Apple's wording. DisplayPort on the port is what a driver-free USB-C portable monitor uses; no DisplayLink-type driver is involved on this laptop.

findings.label: External displays the 16-inch MacBook Pro drives
findings.value: M5 Pro: up to three external displays, each up to 6K at 60 Hz or 4K at 144 Hz, over any combination of Thunderbolt and HDMI; M5 Max: up to four
findings.note: A 2560x1600 panel at 120 Hz or 144 Hz has fewer pixels than 4K at 144 Hz, so it is inside Apple's stated limit; the comparison is mine. Dual-screen extenders (two added screens) are also inside the count on both chips.

findings.label: Separate charging port and included charger
findings.value: MagSafe 3 port in addition to the three Thunderbolt 5 ports and an HDMI port; 140W USB-C Power Adapter included
findings.note: Because charging has its own port, the charger need not pass through the monitor. A monitor's pass-through figure (65 W on the Duex Float 2 Pro per Macworld) matters only if the shopper chooses to charge through the screen, where it is below the 140 W adapter Apple ships.

findings.label: MacBook Pro 16 battery, and what a bus-powered screen costs
findings.note: Arithmetic: each 10 W a screen draws from the Mac is 10 Wh per hour, about 10% of the battery per hour on top of the Mac's own use. At Macworld's 13 W for the espresso Pro 15 that is about 13% per hour (13 / 99.6).

findings.label: Pixel density of the MacBook Pro 16's own screen against portable panels
findings.value: MacBook Pro 16: 3456x2234 at 254 ppi (Apple). 16-inch 2560x1600: about 189 ppi. 15.6-inch 1920x1080: about 141 ppi. 15.6-inch 3840x2160: about 282 ppi
findings.note: Only the 254 ppi figure is Apple's. The others are arithmetic, diagonal pixels divided by diagonal inches: sqrt(2560²+1600²)/16 = 188.7; sqrt(1920²+1080²)/15.6 = 141.2; sqrt(3840²+2160²)/15.6 = 282.4. A 16-inch 2560x1600 panel has about 74% of the MacBook's linear density, a 15.6-inch 1080p panel about 56%.

findings.label: Variable refresh (Adaptive Sync / FreeSync-type) on a Mac: which cable
findings.value: Any Mac with Apple silicon on macOS Monterey 12 or later; 'connect your Adaptive Sync display to the Thunderbolt port of your Mac' with a Thunderbolt, USB-C or other DisplayPort-enabled cable; 'Do not use an HDMI cable or adapter.'
findings.source_title: Use an Adaptive Sync external display with your Mac - Apple Support
findings.note: Page shows a published date of July 16, 2026. Turned on in System Settings > Displays > Refresh Rate > Variable or Adaptive. Apple says it suits gaming and video, may flicker or stutter in other apps, and to pick a fixed rate or ask the display maker if it does.

findings.label: macOS resolution on an external display
findings.value: 'By default, your Mac automatically uses the best resolution for the display.' 'Using a scaled resolution may affect performance.'
findings.source_title: Change your Mac display's resolution - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's wording, macOS 27 version of the page. It does not mention HiDPI or text sharpness, so it does not by itself support the claim that 1080p text looks soft.

findings.label: Panel and pass-through as Macworld lists them
findings.value: 16-inch, 2560x1600 at 120 Hz, 65W pass-through charging; $299.99 when reviewed
findings.source_title: Best Portable Monitors for Mac 2026: Top lightweight displays for your MacBook | Macworld
findings.note: Macworld's figures, not Mobile Pixels' own; the store page returned HTTP 429 today. The $299.99 is Macworld's review-time price, not today's store price.

findings.label: Which Macs need a display driver for a two-screen extender
findings.value: Macworld: 'plain (non-Pro/Max) M1 and M2 Macs plus the new MacBook Neo are limited to connecting just a single monitor' and need 'free software (rather like DisplayLink)'
findings.source_title: Best Portable Monitors for Mac 2026: Top lightweight displays for your MacBook | Macworld
findings.note: From Macworld's Trio 3 Pro entry. The 16-inch MacBook Pro has only ever shipped with Pro or Max chips in the Apple silicon line-up Apple lists today (M5 Pro, M5 Max), so this limit does not apply to it; that inference is mine.

findings.label: Bus-power draw and pass-through, as Macworld reports them
findings.value: 'the Pro 15 uses around 13W'; passes through up to 100 W to the laptop when the screen has its own charger
findings.source_title: espresso Pro 4K Touch portable monitor review: Genius stand, brilliant screen | Macworld
findings.note: Macworld's figures. Macworld also found brightness better 'when plugged into a wall charger rather than taking power from the laptop'. This is a 4K 60 Hz screen, outside the page's 2560x1600 120 Hz line; it is here only as the one draw figure a named reviewer gives.

findings.label: What a cited rival says about the video path
findings.value: PCWorld: 'We recommend buying a portable monitor that has a USB-C port with DisplayPort Alternate Mode and USB Power Delivery.'
findings.source_title: Best portable monitors 2026: Displays that go with you | PCWorld
findings.note: This is the part of the mechanism a rival already has. It gives no Mac-side limit, no watt figure for the laptop port and nothing on HDMI versus USB-C for variable refresh.

unsourced: How many watts a 16-inch MacBook Pro Thunderbolt 5 port supplies to a bus-powered screen. Apple's specs page and MacBook Pro guide give no figure. Intel's Thunderbolt 5 technology brief (search snippet: 'Minimum PC port power for accessories 15W') downloaded as a PDF I could not extract text from, and Plugable's Thunderbolt 4 vs 5 article does not state it. So there is no sourced comparison of port output against a screen's draw.
